items.title: Text question (Types of friction): You push gently on a refrigerator and it does not move; you push harder and it slides across the floor. Identify the type of friction acting in each case.

question.html: Physics idea. When surfaces are not sliding, static friction acts and matches the push (up to a maximum). When they slide, kinetic friction acts. Work. Gentle push, no motion: static friction (equal and opposite to the push). Once the refrigerator slides, the surfaces move relative to each other: kinetic friction.

answer.html: Static friction while it stays at rest; kinetic friction once it slides.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 123): A student claims that dragging a wooden block faster, or on a wider face of the block, increases the friction force. Which factors really determine the sliding friction force?

answer.html: The materials in contact (the coefficient of friction 𝜇) and the normal force pressing the surfaces together: 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>. Speed and contact area do not matter, so the student's claim is wrong.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 123): Why should bicycle maintenance include cleaning the brake pads as well as the wheel rims?

question.html: Physics idea. The friction between two surfaces depends on both of them. Contamination on either one lowers 𝜇. Work. A rim brake slows the wheel only through friction at the pad-rim contact. If the pads are coated with oil or dirt, then even a clean rim would give a reduced 𝜇, and the wheel would slide under the pad instead of being gripped. Clean pads on a clean rim restore the full friction force.

answer.html: Friction depends on both surfaces in contact; dirty pads lower the coefficient of friction just as a dirty rim does.

items.title: Compare the friction forces.

question.html: Physics idea. Friction force is 𝐹<sup>𝑓</sup>= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>, so the coefficient between the contacting surfaces matters. Work. 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub><sub>, dry</sub> = (0.18)(800 N) = 1.4 × 10<sup>2</sup> N,

The dry friction is 0.18 / 0.06 = 3 times larger. That extra friction turns motion into heat, wears the metal away, and could make the parts seize. Grease separates the surfaces with a film that slides easily.

answer.html: Dry contact gives about 1.4 × 10<sup>2</sup> N of friction compared with 48 N greased, three times more. Grease is added to cut heat, wear, and wasted energy.

items.title: Check Your Progress 23 (Lesson 2): A hockey puck slides across ice, and a car tire rolls along a dry road without slipping. Identify the type of friction in each, and compare static and kinetic friction.

question.html: Work. Puck: the puck's bottom surface slides on the ice, so kinetic friction acts. Tire: the patch of tire touching the road is momentarily at rest relative to the road (it is rolling, not skidding), so static friction acts, and it is what pushes the car forward. Similar: both act parallel to the surfaces, oppose relative sliding (or its tendency), depend on the materials (𝜇) and on the normal force, and not on contact area. Different: static friction adjusts from zero up to a maximum, 𝐹<sup>𝑓</sup><sup>,</sup><sup> 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑐</sup>≤𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>; kinetic friction has a fixed size 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>. Usually 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>, so a skidding tire grips less than a rolling one.

answer.html: The puck has kinetic friction; the rolling tire has static friction. Both are proportional to 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>; static friction varies up to a maximum 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>, kinetic friction is constant, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>, and usually 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>< 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub> .

items.title: Check Your Progress 28 (Lesson 2, Critical Thinking): A box sits on the floor of a delivery van. The coefficient of static friction between the box and the floor is 0.40. The van brakes hard and slows at 5.5 m/s². What force slows the box? Does the box slide, and in which direction relative to the van floor?

question.html: Physics idea. The only horizontal force on the box is friction from the van floor. When the van slows down, static friction pushes the box backward (opposite the motion) to slow it with the van. Work. The largest static friction force is 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔, so the largest deceleration the box can share is

The van slows at 5.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is more than 3.9 m/s<sup>2</sup>, so friction cannot keep up. The box slides toward the front of the van relative to the floor, although relative to the ground it is still slowing down, just not as quickly as the van.

answer.html: Static friction from the floor slows the box. Because 5.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> > 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑔= 3.9 m/s<sup>2</sup>, the box slides forward (toward the cab) relative to the van floor.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 2, p. 123), Why should railway maintenance include wheel cleaning as well as track cleaning?

question.html: Physics idea. The friction between wheel and rail depends on both surfaces. Contamination on either surface lowers 𝜇. Work. A train accelerates and brakes only through friction at the wheel-rail contact. If the wheels carry oil, leaf residue, or grease, then even clean rails would have a reduced 𝜇 and the wheels would slip when starting and slide when braking. Clean wheels on clean rails restore the full friction force.

answer.html: Friction depends on both surfaces in contact; dirty wheels would reduce the coefficient of friction and traction/braking just as dirty tracks do.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect, Do steel components touch directly in a vehicle? What if they did? (Table 2)

question.html: Physics idea. Friction force is 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>, so the coefficient between the contacting surfaces matters. Work. Table 2: steel on steel has 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.78 and 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.42, large values. Moving parts (pistons, bearings, gears) that touched bare would experience large friction forces, wasting energy as heat, wearing out, and possibly seizing. Steel on steel with castor oil has 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.15 and 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.08, about 5 times smaller. So designers separate moving steel parts with lubricant (or bearings) rather than letting them touch dry.

answer.html: Steel parts that move against each other are normally separated by a lubricant film. Bare steel on steel (𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.42) would produce about five times more friction than oiled steel (𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.08 ), causing heat, wear, and wasted energy.

question.html: Work. Similar: both act parallel to the surfaces in contact, oppose the (attempted) relative motion, depend on the surface materials (𝜇) and on the normal force, and not on contact area. Different: static friction acts when there is no sliding and adjusts from zero up to a maximum, 𝐹<sup>𝑓</sup><sup>,</sup><sup> 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑐</sup>≤𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>; kinetic friction acts when sliding and has a fixed size 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>. Usually 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>> 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>, so it takes more force to start an object moving than to keep it moving.

answer.html: Both are parallel to the surfaces and proportional to 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> with a material-dependent coefficient. Static friction varies up to a maximum 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup> and acts without sliding; kinetic friction is constant, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>, and acts during sliding (with 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>< 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>).

items.title: Check Your Progress 27 (Lesson 2), 13-kg table: 20 N does not move it; 25 N gives a = 0.26 m/s². What can you conclude about the coefficients?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 13 kg, so 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔= 127 N. Physics idea. Case 1: at rest, so static friction = 20 N ≤𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>. Case 2: the table moves, so the maximum static friction was exceeded, and kinetic friction acts: 𝐹−𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑚𝑎. Work.

Also, since 25 N started the table moving, 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>< 25 N, so 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>< 25 / 127 = 0.20. Combined with 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>< 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub> for typical surfaces, 0.17 < 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>< 0.20.

answer.html: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>≈0.17 and 0.16 ≤𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>< 0.20 (the static coefficient is somewhat larger than the kinetic one, about 0.17 to 0.20).

items.title: Check Your Progress 28 (Lesson 2, Critical Thinking), Rachel's dresser in a truck: what accelerates it? When could it slide, and which way?

question.html: Physics idea. The only horizontal force on the dresser is friction from the truck bed. When the truck accelerates forward, static friction pushes the dresser forward with it. Work. The largest static friction force is 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑚𝑔, so the largest acceleration the dresser can share is 𝑎<sup>𝑚𝑎𝑥</sup>= 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑔. If the truck accelerates faster than 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑔 (or the bed is slick, wet, or oily), friction cannot keep up and the dresser slides. The dresser then moves backward relative to the truck bed (toward the tailgate), although relative to the ground it still moves forward, just not as fast as the truck.

answer.html: Static friction between the bed and the dresser accelerates it forward. It slides if the truck's acceleration exceeds 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝑔 (or the bed is slippery), and it slides toward the rear of the truck relative to the bed.
